title: llm-gemini 0.38
text: Release: llm-gemini 0.38 Today Google introduced Gemini 4 Neon . I wrote recently about how confusing the pricing for the Gemini 4 series was - Neon has somehow made this even worse. Previously the Gemini 4 lineup was Hydrogen, Argon, and Carbon - where Argon and Carbon were the same price , and Hydrogen was 3/4 of that price now but will be 1/4 of that price when the other two double an 1st December once their initial discount pricing expires. The Neon announcement pretends that Argon doesn't exist. Here's their new image explaining the model line-up: So the lineup now, from most to least expensive, is Carbon, Neon, Hydrogen. Except Carbon is currently half price, so right now Neon ($3/million input, $15/million output) is the most expensive of the three - then Carbon ($2/$10), then Hydrogen ($1.50/$7.50). I guess this will make more sense when Carbon doubles to $4/$20 on December 1st. I ran some pelicans through the three reasoning levels for Neon - low, medium, high. I dropped Argon from my Gemini 4 comparison grid - here's the new Gemini 4 lineup, where the Neon pelicans do look better than Hydrogen and worse than Carbon: As I've done with several recent models , I also fired the following prompt against Gemini 4 Neon on "extra" effort level in Google Antigravity: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's the result . title: Why I prefer on-site over online training
author: Bas Dijkstra
text: I’ve been running workshops and training courses for close to 10 years now, and in that time, I have had the pleasure of working with teams on pretty much every continent, both on technical, hands-on programming courses as well as more strategical workshops. One important lesson I have learned from all these sessions is that in-person training is generally much more effective than online courses There are a number of reasons for this. Group work is easier to facilitate Most of the workshops and training courses I run involve some kind of work to be done in small groups of typically 2-4 people. This could be coming up with testing ideas, reviewing an existing automation code base, pairing up to solve a programming problem, discussing the next steps for a test automation strategy, or something else. Doing these tasks in small groups improves the quality of the discussions, because people learn not just from me, but also from their peers in the workshop or course. And while most online teaching platforms offer support for working in small groups through break-out rooms, it’s simply not the same experience as gathering around a flipover or a screen and discussing the task at hand. Engagement is easier to gauge I pride myself on the ability to adapt my courses and workshops to the particular learning requirements of the group I’m working with. That does not just mean creating a bespoke curriculum through one or more discovery call(s) before the workshop or course, but I also frequently adapt both the content and the pace of the workshop on the fly, based on the feedback of the participants. That feedback might be explicit, for example when someone asks me to cover a specific question, tool or technique that did not come up in the discovery calls. If time and opportunity allows for it, I’m always happy to do so, and the feedback I get afterwards often reflects that. Feedback might come to me in a more implicit way, too, though. If I see a large part of the group struggling with the problems at hand, I can slow the pace or clarify things that are unclear. If I see people fiddling with their phones or being otherwise disengaged, I can address that by increasing the pace or introducing additional topics and problems for them to work on. Both types of feedback, but especially the implicit type, is much harder to get when running an online course. I can’t see body language very easily, I can’t see if people are doing other things than working on the problems as easily, and that means I can’t use that feedback to improve their learning experience. Sure, I will ask them explicitly if they’re happy with the pace and the content several times throughout the day (I make a habit of doing this in all my sessions no matter if it is on-site or online), but experience tells me that people are much more reluctant to tell me where I can improve things in an online session. It’s easier to help someone out if they’re stuck This one applies specifically to hands-on programming exercises, which make up a significant part of most of my workshops and courses. If someone is stuck, and we’re in the same room, I can easily walk over to where they’re sitting and point out where the error is if I see it. This could be anywhere from a missing semicolon or closing bracket to changing a sequence of method calls. Sure, I can do something similar in an online session by asking the participant in question to share their screen, but this is a lot more intrusive to the learning process. There’s some technical friction (sharing permissions, people searching for the sharing button and the windows they want to share), but because - at least that’s what I assume - everybody hears everything I say, the people who are not a part of the problem-solving conversation still hear me discuss this, which causes a distraction. title: Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) – An open-source developer tool for designers
author: D_R_Farrell
text: Hey HN, I'm Daniel, founder of Onlook ( https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook and onlook.com). Onlook is a desktop app that puts a canvas on top of your real codebase, letting you design directly in code with the agent you already use. Over 25,000 designers and developers have supported the project, 100+ have contributed, and it's been the #1 trending repo in the world twice. We just rebuilt the entire product as an agentic design tool, and open-sourced it to the community. Here’s a demo video: ( https://youtu.be/BogcYWf4siM ) If you're an engineer, traditional engineering tools are largely built for convergence, whereas designers tend to explore and diverge on ideas. Onlook gives designers a familiar canvas while managing all of the dev processes that get between them and making mind-blowing designs in code. Designers can work on a multiple simultaneous worktrees that run on the real app locally, and every change lands as a PR you can review or throw away, so there aren’t mockups to rebuild. We built Onlook because we believe there needs to be a developer tool that works the way designers do. More and more, designers are expected to work in code. Designers think by seeing, drafting, arranging variations, using references, and remixing ideas. That’s why the canvas has been the signature feature of design tools because it genuinely is useful for how messy the creative process is. Most of the challenge of using engineering tools for design work is that the first half of starting a project often takes mental bandwidth in of itself (What branch am I on? What page was that last exploration on?) and the second half is constrained by configuring your coded design to present itself (prompting design tools on top of what you’ve built or making temporary navigation for that specific state). Some of you may remember our earlier Show HNs (July 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40904862 , August 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41390449 , May 2025: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44127653 ). Since then, we built a web version (too early), then a Storybook-native build (a mistake). We noticed that our desktop product from July 2024 was still getting hundreds of downloads a month despite zero promotion, so we decided to rebuild it for the new era of designers working in code. How it works… Onlook shines at exploring tons of ideas at once. Ask it to lay out every flow in your product, show every state of a component, or riff on ten versions of one screen. Your designs all show up side by side on an infinite canvas, with each frame as a real webview running your actual app with real data. Not as a mockup, but the real deal. When we built this editor, we had an epiphany that it could be a new kind of IDE for design. Design tools used to be limited to a proprietary setup or closed schema, but now you can push and pull the medium of code to get whatever result you want, so why not give agents an infinite canvas of browsers and see what they do? It turns out, the agents can figure out how to better present coded work by adjusting the urls of browser frames and arranging and resizing them on the canvas. The concept is simple, but it requires a lot of product thinking. For example, because all of the frames on the canvas share a single browser session, and Chromium only allows six connections per host per session, ten frames of the same app end up fighting over limited connections. So, we had to plan around that, and there are still tons of things we need to do to make the canvas ultra performant. Onlook is an Electron app where you can import a repo from GitHub or upload a local folder. Then, Onlook creates a git worktree, starts your dev server, and has the agent sort out missing dependencies or other requirements. You never open a terminal and everything the agent does is a normal git diff that can go to GitHub as a PR. title: Show HN: Robotics needs better CAD, so I wrote a B-rep kernel and 3,487 tests
author: atomarch
text: Hey HN, I’m Tony. I’m a co-founder of Springcraft, where we have been doing a lot of CAD modeling for robot parts. Our team kept running into limitations with existing kernels, and so I decided to write a new B-rep kernel and a new comprehensive, kernel-agnostic B-rep conformance test suite. Both are available today under MIT licenses. The kernel, springrep, is written in safe Rust with no dependencies. It covers a broad range of our mechanical CAD needs, including advanced fillets, sweeps, lofts, shells, offsets, STEP and exact measurements and queries. Claude Code made it feasible to write this, but it took a lot of time and care to get it right. The test suite, brep-conformance, has 3,487 cases covering the modeling operations common across kernels: booleans, fillets, chamfers, shells, offsets, sweeps, lofts, STEP, and queries with expected answers coming from closed forms and exact geometry. It caught hundreds of bugs, edge cases, and hot spots in springrep that our own tests had missed, and now springrep passes all of it. We’ve also run it on a few popular open-source kernels and anyone can run it on theirs. This is the first version, so there are surely mistakes in the test and adapters. Corrections, pull requests, and new kernels are welcome. kernel: https://github.com/springcraft-ai/springrep conformance suite: https://springcraft-ai.github.io/brep-conformance/

title: Show HN: An API for word timestamps from speech, 75% within 20ms
author: jasperstory
text: Hey HN, we're Yarn (W24) and we make a video editing app for startups, and we built Quebec ( https://quebec.yarn.so ), an API that gives you accurate word timestamps from speech. We needed it because cutting a word even 50ms off from its true timing can ruin talking head footage (examples in the write up). Accurate word timestamps usually come from a forced aligner, which takes the speech audio and a transcript and works out exactly when each word starts and ends. We weren't satisfied with the accuracy of Montreal Forced Aligner (MFA) or new models like ElevenLabs Cue ( https://elevenlabs.io/blog/cue-aligner ). Giving LLMs access to a waveform/spectrogram didn't help much either. So we built our own. There are two particularly interesting parts: - We wrote our own decoder around MFA's acoustic model that only lets each word land within 200ms of the rough timings. That made search small enough to solve exactly, so we don't need to use MFA's beam search. - We added a small CNN, built on the first two layers of Whisper Tiny, that nudges each word boundary by up to 50ms. We couldn't find enough hand-labelled speech that allowed for commercial use, so we had Gemini label our own (17k word boundaries). It took a couple of hours and cost under $200. A net trained on Gemini's labels scored the same as one trained on human labels (73.9% vs. 74%). One way to measure accuracy is % of word boundaries within 20ms of hand labels. Here are the results on Buckeye (hand-labelled American speech that we didn't train on): - Quebec 75% - MFA 61% - ElevenLabs Cue 30% If you want to try it, it's free until tomorrow night. You can point your agent at our docs at https://quebec.yarn.so , and send audio on its own or with your own transcript. After that, it costs $0.32 per hour with no signup (minimum $10 top-up). We serve it at cost. Caveats: only tested in English and slower than ElevenLabs. Let us know if Quebec works well for you, and send us any samples that work badly (you can email support at yarn dot so). Also let us know if you've built or found a better aligner. In theory we would just switch to a better aligner, although we would probably just push a bit harder to make ours better. Thanks! Jasper
